chapter.title: A Room Nobody Can Reach
chapter.sub: A witness who can't hear, a control nobody can reach, and an interpreter in the dark.
chapter.status: **DRAFT** · scripted from the series plan · IDs provisional

items.text: SEASON 6 · EPISODE 4 · DRAFT · CASE-033  Design review · Maya, Farah, Odile and Judge Obi · Level L4 · Intermediate support  Courtroom 3 works — for someone who can hear, reach and see. Farah’s design review finds three people it doesn’t work for.  ⚑ RV-143: access decided with disabled users and the reviewer; reach tables differ by jurisdiction. RV-141: figures illustrative. Some choices run on a clock.

items.title: A Room Nobody Can Reach
items.stakes: Farah's design review blocks Courtroom 3: a witness who can't hear, a control nobody in a wheelchair can reach, and an interpreter in the dark.
items.reward: A courtroom everyone can take part in — tested with the people it's for.

objectives.text: Fund the review within the budget
Look closer: two things about the review

items.rumor: The room worked perfectly for someone who could hear, reach and see — which wasn't everyone.

items.alt: In a full-size courtroom mock-up, Farah — the accessibility reviewer — points at the witness box. Maya holds the assisted-listening plan.

bubbles.text: Your assisted-listening plan covers every position but one.

items.caption: The witness box. Where a person answers questions under oath.

lines.text: You covered every seat in the gallery. The one person who has to answer questions under oath can't hear them.
‘Witnesses can ask on the day’ was in the brief.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #55 · AVERY'S LENS  Design for the edges, not the average  If the person with the least hearing, the lowest reach or no sound at all can use the room, everyone can.  Courtroom 3 worked for an average participant. The witness who couldn't hear, the lawyer who couldn't reach and the juror who couldn't see her interpreter weren't average.

items.alt: Courtroom 3's access plan: bench, jury box, counsel and gallery outlined in green as covered; the witness box in red, uncovered; the interpreter's circle in a dark far corner.
items.caption: Three of four positions — and an interpreter nobody can see.

items.prompt: I've reviewed a lot of courtrooms. Want to know the question I ask first?

options.label: “Who can't take part in this room — and where are they sitting?”
options.reply: That's the one. Start there and the checklist writes itself.

options.label: “Is it code compliant?”
options.reply: Code is the floor. People are the brief.

options.label: “What do most courts do?”
options.reply: Most courts have the same gaps. Ask a better question.

items.prompt: 9:30. Farah's first comment: no assisted listening at the witness box. Your answer?
items.risk: A witness who can't hear the question.

hints.text: Who sits at each position — and what do they need?

options.label: “Witnesses can ask for a receiver on the day”
options.result: Farah: “If they don't know to ask, they don't hear the question.”
options.fail: A requirement isn't a favour on the day.

options.label: Cover the witness box — then list every position and check each one
options.result: Four positions; the witness box was the only gap in coverage. The list finds two more problems.

options.label: Point out that the code only requires a percentage of seats
options.consequence: A number that leaves out the person who matters most.

options.label: Add a sign at the entrance
options.result: Now people know the witness box has nothing.

items.title: Out of reach.
items.body: The position list turns up comment 2: the counsel lectern's touch panel. Top control at 1.52 m, behind a 500 mm deep top. Farah's reach table allows 1.22 m forward. A lawyer in a wheelchair couldn't start the evidence display.
items.label: Test: what's the fix — and whose table decides?
**Fix it:** fund Farah's review inside the change budget.

items.title: The Deaf President Now protest
items.body: In March 1988, students at Gallaudet University in Washington, D.C. — a university for deaf and hard-of-hearing students — shut down the campus for a week until the board appointed the university's first deaf president. The protest's lesson is often quoted in design reviews: decisions about access are better made with the people who need it, not for them.

items.prompt: Tuesday. The panel is 0.3 m out of reach. What do you draw?
items.risk: A lawyer who can't present her own evidence.
timeout: The first wheelchair-using lawyer finds out in court.

hints.text: Which table — and can anyone reach it without help?

options.label: Top control at 1.2 m on a side-approachable mount, and a second control at the clerk's desk; confirm with Farah and Odile
options.result: Farah signs comment 2 off; Odile adjusts the lectern.
options.consequence: In reach, and not dependent on anyone.

options.label: A step stool at the lectern
options.result: Farah: “A stool is not a reach range.”
options.fail: Move the control, not the person.

options.label: The clerk will press it for them
options.result: The lawyer now depends on the clerk for her own evidence.

options.label: Put the panel at 0.4 m
options.result: Now it's out of reach standing and seated.

items.title: In the dark.
items.body: Comment 3: the sign-language interpreter's position is a corner behind the witness box. The mock-up reads 30 lux on her face, the deaf juror can't see her from the jury box, and the camera for remote interpreting points at a wall.
items.label: Test: who can't use the room — and what does the position need?

items.prompt: Tuesday afternoon. Where does the interpreter go?
items.happening: Interpreter unlit and out of sight.
items.risk: A deaf juror shut out of the trial.
timeout: The response goes out without comment 3.

hints.text: Who needs to see her, and who decides where she stands?

options.label: Into the sightlines of the jury, the witness and the bench, with light on face and hands and a camera position; agreed with Odile, the court and deaf users
options.result: Odile moves a railing; Judge Obi approves the sightline from the bench; the mock-up test passes.
options.consequence: A signal path that happens to be a person.

options.label: Leave her where she is and add a spotlight
options.result: Lit — and still out of sight of the jury.

options.label: Put her next to the judge's bench
options.result: Judge Obi: “The interpreter can't stand where she looks like part of the court.”
options.consequence: The court's procedure is the court's.

options.label: Replace her with automatic captions
options.result: Captions aren't a sign-language interpreter; the deaf juror signs.
options.consequence: A different service, not a replacement.

items.label: **Service Mode:** answer the design review yourself.

items.sub: Intermediate · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Farah and Maya beside a board. Percent is part over whole, times a hundred. How many of the courtroom's positions can a hard-of-hearing person use? Gallery, counsel tables, jury box… not the witness box. Three of four positions: seventy-five percent. And the witness box is where the person whose words matter most sits.

items.alt: The revised plan: all five positions outlined in green, the interpreter's circle moved into the sightlines between the jury box and the witness box, lit.
items.caption: Four of four. Seen, lit, in reach.

items.title: 1.22 m forward
items.body: Farah's review uses the jurisdiction's reach table: 1.22 m for a forward reach, a little more for a side reach — if a wheelchair can pull alongside. The counsel lectern's panel faces forward, over a 500 mm deep top. Nobody could pull alongside.

items.alt: Farah and Maya after the mock-up test with a hard-of-hearing witness, a wheelchair user and a deaf juror.

bubbles.text: Three people used your room today. None of them had to ask for anything.

items.title: 30 lux
items.body: The corner Maya drew for the interpreter measured 30 lux on the mock-up — and the deaf juror's seat had a clear view of the witness box's back wall. A sign-language interpreter is a signal path too.

items.alt: Anselm at his desk with a contractor's submittal: an amplifier offered as ‘equal’ to the one specified.

bubbles.text: They say it's equal. Fewer channels, no fault relay, and our spec never said what ‘equal’ means.

items.caption: Next: *Spec vs Submittal.*

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  List every position and who might be there; check assisted listening, reach and sightlines at each one; decide with the reviewer, the architect, the court and disabled users; and prove it in a mock-up with the people it’s for. Percent is part ÷ whole × 100 — but access isn’t a percentage.
REFLECTION (optional)  · Farah asks “who can’t take part in this room?” first. What question do you ask first in your own work?
